lessons.title: A debate: town life or village life?
lessons.objective: Argue for or against town or village life and defend one’s point of view politely.
lessons.course:
In a debate, two teams give reasons for and against an idea. We start with “I think…”, “In my opinion…”, we give reasons with “because”, and we answer the other team politely: “I agree with you, but…”, “I don’t agree because…”.
We speak in turns, we listen, and the chairperson gives the floor.

support.title: Useful phrases
support.text:
In my opinion, village life is better because the air is clean.
I don’t agree, because in town there are hospitals and good roads.
I agree with you, but…

lessons.model: Two adults debate: one says town life is better (electricity, hospitals, jobs), the other says village life is better (clean air, fresh food, family close by).
lessons.guided: Prepare three reasons for your side. Hold a short debate at home or in class with a chairperson.
lessons.exercise: Give one reason why village life can be good.
lessons.answer: For example: the air is clean and the food is fresh.
lessons.remediation: Give one reason with “because” before debating.
lessons.transfer: Ask two adults which they prefer, town or village, and why.

practice.prompt: Which phrase disagrees politely?
Match each reason with the side it supports.
pairs: The air is fresh and clean.

practice.prompt: Say your opinion with a reason.

lessons.title: Reading silently: market day in Kumba
lessons.objective: Read a text silently and answer questions; find synonyms and opposites.
lessons.course:
When we read silently, we read with our eyes, without moving our lips. We read the questions first, then look for the answers in the text.
Synonyms have almost the same meaning (big – large); opposites have contrary meanings (cheap – expensive).

support.title: Read silently
support.text: Wednesday is market day in Kumba. Very early, traders arrive from the villages with plantains, cocoyams and palm oil. The market becomes noisy and crowded. Mrs Mbah sells fresh fish at a fair price, but the imported shoes in the next stall are expensive. By evening, the market is quiet again and the cleaners sweep the alleys.

lessons.model: The adult reads the questions, then reads silently and points to each answer in the text.
lessons.guided: Read the questions, read the text silently and write the answers. Find one synonym and one opposite pair.
lessons.exercise: Which day is market day in Kumba?
lessons.remediation: Read one sentence at a time and ask: who? what? when?
lessons.transfer: Describe your local market day to your family.

practice.prompt: Match each word with its opposite.
What does Mrs Mbah sell?
practice.explanation: The text says she sells fresh fish.

practice.prompt: Find a synonym of “crowded” in the list: full, empty, small.

lessons.title: A persuasive essay: why our town needs a park
lessons.objective: Write a short persuasive essay giving reasons and examples to convince the reader.
lessons.course:
A persuasive essay tries to convince. Plan it:
• Introduction: give your opinion (“Our town needs a public park.”).
• Body: give two or three reasons with examples (“Children need a safe place to play.”).
• Conclusion: repeat your opinion and ask for action (“Let us ask the mayor to build one.”).
Useful words: firstly, secondly, moreover, finally, therefore.
lessons.model: The adult writes the opinion and two reasons on the board, linking them with “Firstly” and “Secondly”.
lessons.guided: Choose a topic (a park, a library, a clean market). Write the opinion, two reasons and a conclusion.
lessons.exercise: Which word can introduce your second reason?
lessons.remediation: Write one opinion sentence and one reason with “because”.
lessons.transfer: Read your essay to an adult and ask whether it convinced them.

practice.prompt: Put the parts of the persuasive essay in order.
items: Firstly, children need a safe place to play.
Therefore, let us ask the mayor to build one.

practice.prompt: Which sentence gives a reason?
choices: Children need a safe place to play.
practice.answer: Children need a safe place to play.

practice.prompt: Write your persuasive essay (about 60 words).
practice.answer: A persuasive essay with an opinion, reasons and a conclusion.

lessons.title: Adjectives: proper adjectives, comparatives and superlatives
lessons.objective: Identify common and proper adjectives and use comparative and superlative forms.
lessons.course:
Common adjectives describe: tall, busy, beautiful. Proper adjectives come from proper nouns and take a capital letter: Cameroon → Cameroonian, Africa → African, England → English.
Comparatives compare two: tall → taller (than), busy → busier, beautiful → more beautiful. Superlatives compare three or more: the tallest, the busiest, the most beautiful.
Irregular: good – better – the best; bad – worse – the worst.
lessons.model: The adult compares: “Douala is bigger than Buea. Douala is the biggest town in the Littoral region.”
lessons.guided: Compare three towns or three buildings with comparatives and superlatives. Write five proper adjectives.
lessons.remediation: Start with short adjectives (tall, small) before longer ones.
lessons.transfer: Compare three things in your village with “-er” and “the -est”.

practice.prompt: Complete the table.
Which one is a proper adjective?
practice.explanation: It comes from Cameroon and takes a capital letter.

practice.prompt: Match each adjective with its superlative.

lessons.title: Intersection and union of sets in the village
lessons.objective: Find the intersection and the union of two sets and use the symbols ∩, ∪ and ∉.
lessons.course:
A = {children who go to the market} = {Ali, Bih, Che}; B = {children who go to the stream} = {Bih, Che, Dzeke}.
Intersection A ∩ B = elements in both sets = {Bih, Che}. Union A ∪ B = all elements of A and B, written once = {Ali, Bih, Che, Dzeke}.
∉ means “is not an element of”: Dzeke ∉ A.
lessons.model: The adult draws two overlapping circles and places the names: the middle part is the intersection.
lessons.guided: Make two sets about activities in your village. Draw them in a Venn diagram and write A ∩ B and A ∪ B.
lessons.remediation: Colour the elements that are in both lists first.
lessons.transfer: Make a Venn diagram of the foods two family members like.
lessons.materials: Two hoops or circles drawn on paper.

practice.prompt: A = {a, b, c}, B = {c, d}. How many elements are in A ∪ B?
practice.explanation: {a, b, c, d}: c is written once.

practice.prompt: Match each symbol with its meaning.
practice.answer: ∩ intersection; ∪ union; ∉ not an element of.

practice.prompt: Draw a Venn diagram of A = {goat, hen, dog} and B = {dog, cat}.
practice.answer: Two circles with “dog” in the middle.
practice.explanation: The common element goes in the intersection.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting up to 5 000 at the market
lessons.objective: Add and subtract four-digit numbers with carrying and borrowing and solve market problems.
lessons.course:
We write numbers in columns (Th H T U) and start with the units. Carry when a column makes 10 or more; borrow when the top digit is smaller.
2 750 + 1 380 = 4 130. 4 000 − 1 275 = 2 725. Check a subtraction with an addition: 2 725 + 1 275 = 4 000.
lessons.model: The adult solves: “Mama sold plantains for 2 350 frs and oranges for 1 475 frs. Total?” in columns: 3 825 frs.
lessons.guided: Solve six market problems in columns. Check each subtraction with an addition.
lessons.remediation: Use bundles and coins to show carrying and borrowing.
lessons.transfer: Add up the cost of three items your family bought at the market.

practice.explanation: Carry in the units, tens and hundreds.

practice.prompt: A trader had 5 000 frs. He spent 2 780 frs. How much is left?
How do we check 4 000 − 1 300 = 2 700?

lessons.title: Perimeter of a rectangle and a square: fencing a garden
lessons.objective: Calculate the perimeter of rectangles and squares.
lessons.course:
The perimeter is the distance all round a shape. Rectangle: P = (length + width) × 2. Square: P = side × 4.
A garden 12 m long and 8 m wide needs (12 + 8) × 2 = 40 m of fence.
lessons.model: The adult walks round a rectangle drawn on the ground and adds the four sides.
lessons.guided: Measure the perimeter of a book, a table and a room. Use the formulas and check by adding the four sides.
lessons.exercise: A square field has sides of 15 m. What is its perimeter?
lessons.remediation: Add the four sides one by one before using the formula.
lessons.transfer: Calculate how much rope is needed to go round your compound’s garden.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is 9 cm long and 5 cm wide. Perimeter in cm?
Which formula gives the perimeter of a square?
practice.explanation: A square has four equal sides.

practice.prompt: A fence of 40 m goes round a square pen. How long is one side, in m?

lessons.title: Grid references and coordinates on a village map
lessons.objective: Locate places on a map using a grid and coordinates.
lessons.course:
A grid divides a map into squares. Columns have letters (A, B, C…) and rows have numbers (1, 2, 3…). The school is in square C2: column C, row 2.
On a coordinate grid, we read across first, then up: the point (3, 4) is 3 across and 4 up.
lessons.model: The adult draws a village map on a 5 × 5 grid and finds the church at B4 and the well at (2, 1).
lessons.guided: Draw a grid map of your quarter with five places. Write their grid references.
lessons.exercise: On a coordinate grid, how do we read (5, 2)?
lessons.remediation: Use a grid on the floor and walk across, then up.
lessons.transfer: Make a treasure map with grid references for a friend.

practice.prompt: We read coordinates…
practice.explanation: Along the corridor, then up the stairs.

practice.prompt: The point (4, 3) moves 2 squares up. What is its new second number?
Draw a grid map of your quarter with five places.
practice.answer: A map with grid letters and numbers.
practice.explanation: Write the reference of each place.
